A LITTLE PREPARATION. A LOT OF LAKE.

Make the lakefront
your own.

You don’t have to travel all 18 miles. Pick a stretch, leave room for a detour, and let the lake set the pace.

18 miBicycle trail
18.5 miPedestrian trail
2 endsArdmore Avenue ↔ 71st Street

The Chicago Park District identifies an 18-mile bicycle trail and an 18.5-mile pedestrian trail, running from Ardmore Avenue in Edgewater to 71st Street on the South Side. They are separate routes in many places. Our atlas shows walking paths as a fine dotted line and cycling paths in terracotta; follow on-site signs for actual travel. Park District trail maps ↗.

Start with a stretch.

For sand and a slower morning

Osterman Beach to Montrose connects the northern beaches with dunes and bird habitat. Leave time for a walking detour through the sanctuary. Bring binoculars if you have them.

For a first look at the skyline

North Avenue to Oak Street is a compact introduction to the city-meets-sand landscape. It is roughly a mile along the shore; your exact distance depends on access points and detours.

For a day of discoveries

Start at Museum Campus, walk toward the Adler skyline viewpoint, and choose an indoor museum or a quiet detour to Northerly Island. Museum tickets and visits are separate from the trail.

For the long view

Promontory Point and 57th Street Beach pair a distinctive limestone shoreline with Hyde Park’s sand. Add Jackson Park only if you have time for an inland detour using designated crossings.

Walking, running, or cycling?

Choose the signed path for your activity where routes separate. Keep right, pass carefully, signal your approach, and slow at beach entrances, bridges, playground approaches, and busy crossings. Stop completely clear of the travel path when taking photographs or checking directions.

For a full-length bicycle ride, pace makes a big difference. At an average of 10 mph, 18 miles takes about 1 hour 48 minutes of riding; stops, crossings, weather, and crowds add time. A 3 mph walk over 18.5 miles takes a little over six hours before breaks. These are arithmetic planning examples, not predicted journey times.

Find your way onto the trail.

Neighborhood access depends on the available bridges, underpasses, and signed crossings. Good starting areas include Ardmore Avenue, Foster Avenue, Montrose Avenue, Fullerton Avenue, North Avenue, Museum Campus, 31st Street, 57th Street, and 63rd Street. Use the official section maps ↗ to locate the appropriate connector for your activity.

Lake Shore Drive separates many inland attractions from the shore. A nearby marker is not an invitation to cross a roadway directly. The atlas distinguishes stops on the trail, connector destinations, and nearby detours.

Water, restrooms & a beach break.

Bring drinking water, particularly on a longer outing. Beach houses and park facilities are useful places to check for restrooms, but seasonal operations and individual opening hours vary. The Park District lists restrooms at Margaret T. Burroughs Beach ↗; check the facility before relying on it. This atlas does not mark unverified drinking fountains as available.

Swimming is permitted only in designated areas during the official beach season and when lifeguards are on duty. Use the Park District’s beach information ↗ and posted conditions for the day. Beach sand and water access are different from the paved trail, including for people using mobility devices.

Getting there—and home.

A one-way outing can work well with transit. Consult CTA’s current trip planner ↗ for routes, service, station accessibility, and bicycle policies. Check your return before setting out, especially when finishing in a different neighborhood.

Divvy ↗ offers shared bicycles around Chicago. Use its live service for station availability, vehicle rules, and current pricing. Plan a place to end the rental; a bicycle drawn in the atlas does not indicate an available dock.

The lake has its own weather.

Mornings can bring softer light and a quieter trail, while sunny weekends and events draw crowds. Wind and temperature at the shoreline can feel different from the streets inland. Pack sun protection and a layer suited to the forecast. In winter, ice and exposed edges can change access; in spring and fall, the natural areas reward a slower visit during bird migration.

Check the National Weather Service Chicago forecast ↗ and follow closures, wave warnings, and on-site instructions. The illustrated map does not provide live conditions.

OFFICIAL UPDATE · REVIEWED NOVEMBER 18, 2026

Trail maintenance

The Park District’s notice dated September 14–15, 2026 describes staged trail repairs beginning in the south and progressing north. Work locations and access can change. Read the original maintenance notice and current official updates ↗ before visiting; this is a dated summary, not a live closure map.

Make room for the quiet places.

Stay on marked paths in natural areas, respect habitat fences, and watch wildlife without feeding or approaching it. In a sanctuary, a patient few minutes can reveal more than a hurried circuit. The trail will still be there when you are ready to move on.
